Circle Triplet

GeometryCirclesConstructions
Game: This is a drawing, not a game: three half-circles make a shoemaker's knife, and three circles tucked inside it turn out to be exactly the same size.
How to play: Drag A, B or C along the bottom line, or focus a point and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show names or the inversion hint.
Look for the math

Move the middle point and the three circles change size together. However you stretch the arbelos, the two small twin circles and a third circle found from them keep exactly the same radius. Here is why, and how to see the third one.

The shoemaker's knife

An arbelos is what is left inside the big semicircle on AB when the two smaller semicircles on AC and CB are cut away. Write r1 = AC/2, r2 = CB/2 and R = r1 + r2. The perpendicular through C meets the big arc at D. Archimedes proved in his Book of Lemmas that the two circles drawn between that line and each small arc have the same radius p = r1·r2/R; these are the twins W₁ and W₂.

The circle that touches all three

Proposition 6 puts a circle (O₃) inside the arbelos touching all three semicircles. If r = CB/AC, Archimedes found its diameter is AB·r/(1+r+r²). In our radii that is R3 = R·r1·r2/(r1² + r1·r2 + r2²). The logic test checked this on 1,089 arbeloses and also checked that (O₃) really touches all three arcs: it does in every case.

The third of the triplets

Let K and L be the points where (O₃) touches the two small semicircles. The circumcircle of the triangle K, L, C is the brother circle W₃ found by L. Bankoff in 1974. Its centre sits directly above C on the line CD, and its radius is p = r1·r2/R — the very same as the twins. The task asked us to check that claim rather than copy it: an independent circumcircle computation agreed with the formula to better than a millionth in all 1,089 cases, both for the circle above the baseline and for its mirror image below it (dashed here).

Why inversion sees it

Invert about A with power AC·AB. This swaps B and C, so the small circle on AC becomes a line standing at B and the big circle becomes a line standing at C; the other small circle is unchanged. The twins and W₃ turn into circles wedged between two lines and one circle, which makes their equal radii easy to read off. Tick Inversion hint to see the inversion circle and the four image circles; the dashed reflections are the mirror view the old applet used.

The applet and this page

The original applet found its tangent circles with an Apollonius solver, using enormous circles (radius a million) to stand in for the perpendicular through C, and shifted the big circle one pixel down so its solver would not divide by zero. It drew the circle below the baseline. Here the same circles are computed from the exact formulas, so the equal radii are exact and both copies can be shown. The logic test rebuilds the applet's own calculation method for method and confirms it agrees with these formulas to within a small fraction of the picture's width.

Try dragging C to the middle: the three equal circles grow as large as they can, with radius R/4.
